title: Xu Zhiyuan, Once a Feverish Young Man, Talks About the Early Internet | 1999 Memoirs, Part 7
excerpt: We interviewed a few of the earliest chroniclers of China's internet, hoping to rebuild that era through them.
body:
We interviewed a few of the earliest chroniclers of China's internet, hoping to rebuild that era through them.

**China's business landscape today was shaped almost entirely by companies founded 20 years ago. No one saw that coming.**

**Sohu, founded in August 1996.**

**NetEase, founded in June 1997.**

**Tencent, founded on November 11, 1998.**

**Sina, founded on November 30, 1998.**

**Alibaba, founded in April 1999.**

**Trip.com Group, founded in May 1999.**

**Dangdang, founded in November 1999.**

**Shanda, founded in November 1999**

**……**

**On this incomplete map of internet startups in 1999, we can pick out the companies that still matter today:**

**NetEase had the most-visited site of the moment,** **and its email and personal-homepage businesses were booming**. **William Ding, 28, hurried from Guangzhou to Beijing to collect an award; four years later he would sit at the top of the Hurun Rich List.**

**Zhang Chaoyang graduated from MIT and came back to Beijing to become the most famous internet entrepreneur of his generation. He renamed his company "Sohu," which had a nice echo of that internet legend "Yahoo."**

**Wang Zhidong was named president and CEO of Sina. His biggest achievement until then had been developing a Chinese-language Windows platform and founding Stone Rich Sight, a company built on software. Now he was turning to the internet business, less than a year before Sina listed on Nasdaq.**

**Tencent launched an instant-messaging program called OICQ, later renamed QQ. It was not the only product on the market with a name like that — all of them copied ICQ, made by an Israeli company. OICQ was sluggish at first. Two years later, in an office in Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei, Pony Ma was losing sleep over fundraising.**

**Jack Ma came back to Hangzhou from Beijing. Alibaba's business was still unclear, but he made the cover of *Forbes* the following year. What people remembered about him most was that his English was good.**

**Trip.com Group was founded in Shanghai; among its co-founders was Neil Shen, a master of capital markets.**

**Dangdang copied Amazon and started selling books online. The next year, Kingsoft, with Lei Jun as general manager, turned Joyo.com's main business into an online bookstore as well.**

**That same November, Shanda Networking was founded. Two years later, *The Legend of Mir 2*, the Korean online game Shanda held the exclusive license for, would redefine what popularity and addiction meant.**

**Behind these companies stands a crowd of peers and rivals who vanished and were forgotten. Some had a moment of glory and then went quiet; others rewrote the rules of the game and were overturned by the next wave of innovators…**

**We interviewed a few of the earliest chroniclers of China's internet, hoping to rebuild that era through them.**

**Some of them compare it to Woodstock. Some remember a freedom, an absence of limits, that had never existed before. Some praise the entirely new way of building wealth.**

**"Courage" and "persistence" were the words that came up most, more often even than "ideals." And, of course, "luck."**

**But others think that what looks unimaginable now felt perfectly ordinary at the time; the people who later became startup heroes and models of wealth were just ordinary people standing next to you, and back then you could not have picked them out.**

**We are publishing these chroniclers' oral accounts and their own stories one by one. This is the seventh.**

In 2001, Xu Zhiyuan, then 25, published two collections of essays. *Those Melancholy Young Men* (《那些忧伤的年轻人》) took its name from F. Scott Fitzgerald's short-story collection *All the Sad Young Men*. Before the Depression arrived, Fitzgerald wrote about young love and American high-society parties over and over, and never tired of it.

The other, *The Nasdaq Generation* (《纳斯达克的一代》), sounded like a cover story in *The Economist* or *The Atlantic*. Marc Andreessen was the emblem of the Nasdaq generation; he was 24 when he invented the Netscape browser. That August, Netscape's IPO made him a very rich man.

![Marc Andreessen](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201903182348237owMnJFiIxHm0OjP.jpg-w600)

"What interests me is how a young man with no backing but plenty of ambition wins honor, wealth and beautiful women," Xu Zhiyuan wrote in the book's afterword. In China, people found a similar idol in Zhang Chaoyang, a graduate of MIT. Speaking at Tsinghua University on April 8, 2000, Sohu's chief executive said: "The internet is a bubble that will never burst." Xu put that line at the top of his afterword.

In 1999, singing the praises of youth and internet culture was the most natural thing in the world. "In the summer of 1999 the air in Beijing was full of that itch to act. I suddenly noticed that my classmates had all started debating whether to drop out and start a company, and at Sculpting in Time, the café by Peking University's east gate that used to be packed with literary and artistic youth, what fashionable young men and women said most often was, 'I'm building a website.'"

In 1999, Xu Zhiyuan took a year's leave from Peking University's Department of Microelectronics. He began writing for newspapers and magazines, hoping to become someone like Walter Lippmann or Henry Luce and found a publication with enormous influence. His prose was bold and worldly, and he knew American culture down to the last detail. That winter he joined a startup of about 50 people that wanted to build a Chinese *GQ* — an online one. His declaration was sincere and slightly theatrical: "I firmly believe the happiest time of my life was the first three months at that company." The following May, Xu quit. His new employer was eLong, an internet company founded in 1999. eLong was growing fast, but what won him over was the loose Silicon Valley manner and American backgrounds of its two founders.

By 2001, though, things had turned complicated and confusing. The internet bubble had burst; the Nasdaq index, having reached 5,048 points, had begun a long slide. Mary Meeker, the Wall Street star analyst who had helped push Netscape's shares from $18 to $171, had been celebrated for saying that "pageviews matter more than short-term profit, eyeballs matter more than financial health" — now she was the target of everyone's anger. The Chinese startups Sohu and NetEase went public on Nasdaq in what was called a "bloodletting listing." NetEase was suspended from trading in August 2001 for filing false financial statements. And Wang Zhidong, the 34-year-old technology prodigy out of Zhongguancun, had just been kicked off the board of Sina, the company he built.

Everyone felt it: "the formal end of the adolescence of China's internet industry." The United States was no different. *Business 2.0*, the new-economy magazine that used to sit on the desks of every tech elite, thick enough to "kill a man if it fell on him," ran "100 fewer pages of advertising in the December 26 [2000] issue than in the one before it."

Even so, young people's wish to "become part of the world" did not deflate along with the internet bubble. Because "it would be foolish to measure this movement by business alone." Because "I admit we were dazzled by wealth, but what mattered more was that we found our view of life startlingly torn open," Xu Zhiyuan wrote.

"I want to become part of the world" — the country wanted much the same thing at the time. China had filed its application in 1986 with the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the predecessor of the World Trade Organization. By 1999, 15 years of talks — the longest in the organization's history — had reached the final stretch. With the United States alone there had already been 25 rounds.

In those years nearly every Chinese internet company found itself a wildly successful American company to model itself on. That wave of imitation ran for more than a decade, easing only a little when the mobile internet arrived.

But the cracks had already shown in 1999. On May 8 that year, five munitions fired by American bombers hit the Chinese embassy in Belgrade, causing casualties. Anti-American demonstrations broke out across the country, with young students in front. Once the marches ended, though, they seemed to carry on with their plans as before. In 1998, 17,622 people went abroad to study; by 2000 the figure had more than doubled, to 38,989. More than 10,000 of them went to the United States.

Early this March, we met Xu Zhiyuan in Beijing. His days are full now. Partly it is because One Way Street, the bookstore he founded, is busy adding shops and business lines. He is also a producer of the much-argued-over interview show *Thirteen Invitations* (《十三邀》), and plans to launch another program soon. Gripped by the history of China's transformation at the turn of the 20th century, Xu is also writing a book about Liang Qichao.

As he did years ago, he still believes "it would be foolish to measure this movement by business alone," and he wanted to discuss the internet's development in 1999 and over the 20 years since through "the relationship between the state and society." That inevitably meant touching the "elephant in the room," which made saying what he thought painful.

We have kept the conversation as close to its original form as we could.

**Q: I think everyone had some imagined version of America back then, but yours seems to have been different from the entrepreneurs'. I'd like to start with those different ways of imagining America in 1999. In what frame of mind did you watch the internet boom?**

For me it was of course part of a larger enlightenment. This particular enlightenment was driven by technology and capital — for China, and for me. Silicon Valley showed me another world. Before that I had probably been formed by the liberal culture of 1960s America; the American culture I loved most was probably New England culture, the culture of Emerson (Ralph Waldo Emerson) in the 19th century — real individualism, finding the self, understanding more fully the relationship between the self and the outside world. Many waves have driven changes like that. It started with Kant saying, dare to use your own reason.

![Ralph Waldo Emerson, who in 1835 founded the "Transcendental Club" with a group of intellectuals. He held to his belief in the "infinite individual" into old age. Image from [Wikipedia](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ralph_Waldo_Emerson_ca1857_retouched.jpg)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20190318233850iKJMCAp3cvyPaG7s.jpg-w600)

The 1980s were an enlightenment in China too. Theirs came through Nietzsche, through Freud, through that humanist thought. Mine, in the 1990s, came through Silicon Valley's new technology, new ways of working and new spirit of equality, including the equal distribution of information.

Of course I was excited. It meant possibility for young people. I can't quite reproduce that feeling; you can read the piece I wrote at the time, "I Was Once a Dot-Commer" (《我曾是一个 dot-commer》) — the excitement of a young man. Before, I could only look at that world through the five-yuan copies of *Time* I bought in a warehouse at Peking University; then all at once the internet showed me a far wider world, and young businessmen. Zhang Chaoyang was someone I admired enormously back then — a young man who could change China's business environment that directly. That was a huge encouragement. He gave off a kind of egalitarian spirit.

**Q: In that piece you mention interviewing Zhang Chaoyang. You were at *PC Life* then, and you wrote that you wanted Zhang to know that "the young reporter in front of you is China's future Walter Lippmann. All you did was create China's Yahoo."**

Ha. When you're young you always have a certain pride in yourself. Looking back, Lippmann wasn't really that important, but at the time he was a crucial reference point for me. So for us Zhang Chaoyang wasn't only a business figure. Back then he was an enlightener, and that mattered enormously. He brought a new voice, new ideas into China. I've always thought that was remarkable.

That first wave — people like Zhang Chaoyang and Tian Suning — all carried a strong sense of enlightenment. After 2000 it slowly turned into a normal business form; its newness faded, and the more vigorous, more open qualities thinned out. By now the internet has become a giant business. It no longer holds the old spirit, which is natural enough.

In the early stage it is bound to be livelier, more willing to break through walls. That's true everywhere in the world, and more obvious in China. It created a new frontier, a new space.

**Q: Let's talk about your own 1999. You'd taken leave from school then.**

Right, I took leave. I really couldn't stand going to class anymore — it gave me such headaches — so I went out to find something to do, and started a company more or less by accident. In 1999 I first went to *Sanlian Lifeweek* (《三联生活周刊》) and stayed a few months; a large part of my intellectual taste was formed there. And business never really interested me; what interested me was intellectual experience. Then I went to *PC Life*. And we built a website called Sir. China.

I suddenly felt life held so many possibilities, spiritually and materially. I remember my first job paid 8,000 yuan a month. Think about it: in '99, for someone in his early twenties, 8,000 yuan was a lot of money, maybe several months of my father's salary.

**Q: You'd noticed the wealth side of the "American spirit"?**

Yes, and it was a kind of liberation too. With economic security, your mind can in a sense be more at ease. Later I realized we were only part of a bubble, but the bubble was necessary too, because a bubble gradually turns into something real. That's how China was slowly changed by the internet.

**Q: Why did your company end so quickly?**

I left early, because the money ran out — right when the bubble turned out to be a bubble. What we really wanted was an online *GQ*. So it makes sense that Wang Feng later became the editor of *GQ*. There was an inner logic to it.

**Q: With money, could it have kept going?**

Maybe. There were new sites like that in America at the time too — *Men's Journal*, for instance — going for the feel of an online *GQ*, a new kind of men's magazine that mixed fashion and ideas.

Later I went to eLong. I was content director, running a department of more than 30 people. eLong was a portal site then; only later did it become a pure ticket-booking site. Sina was the thing to aim at. I left after a very short three months, because I'm not suited to office life — I couldn't take it, it gave me headaches. It was already quite free, but it was still a company. Later, when I actually started my own business, I learned that you still have to show up for work; it can never be as free as (the Silicon Valley in those books).

**Q: There were anti-American demonstrations in 1999, and you went.**

That was for the spectacle. I thought it looked fun. I didn't join the march.

**Q: What was the scene like?**

Our school had buses take everyone to Sanlitun. I was curious about why everyone wanted to go, because I knew my classmates all wanted to study in America, were all taking the TOEFL and applying to American universities. I wanted to understand it.

**Q: And what did you make of it?**

Hmm… I think it was the first display of our nationalism. I thought it would be brief, but it turned out to be the start of a long stage. Very two-faced, because, you know, everybody is two-faced. The next day it didn't hold a single one of them up from going to get a visa.

**Q: You didn't want to study in America then?**

I did, but my GPA was too bad. So sometimes I wonder: if I'd gone to study in America when I was younger, would the arc of my life look very different? I don't know.

**Q: You went to America for the first time in 2002, sent by the *Economic Observer* (《经济观察报》) to do interviews. What did it feel like?**

Very familiar, because it was the world I had read about, turned real. There was some dissonance, of course — the world of reading and the real world don't compare exactly — but on the whole it felt intimate and familiar.

**Q: In Hao Chang's *Liang Ch'i-ch'ao and Intellectual Transition in China* (《梁启超与中国思想的过渡》), there's a passage about Liang Qichao arriving in America and finding an enormous gap between what he'd imagined and what was there. He was very disappointed.**

In his day the distance between China and the world was much sharper, cultural differences included. By my time it was less sharp, and now it's less sharp still, not so intense. And I was only there a short time, a month, not enough to form that kind of… I skimmed the surface, visiting a lot of cities.

**Q: A whole crop of business publications appeared in China in those years. The *Economic Observer* had just started too. What did it want to be?**

That was quite clear at the time. We wanted to make a business newspaper for intellectuals.

Our generation, including our founders, who were a bit older than us — by seven, eight, ten years — were still shaped by the enlightenment culture of the 1980s. We still had that consciousness, wanting to bring better and more varied ideas into China. And China at the time was in a state of wanting to be especially open. It had just joined the WTO, and there was a lot to learn from America, from the West. So our newspaper was a bridge back then. We were a hybrid of "the new intellectual and the new-style businessman." Businesspeople and intellectuals ought to have some kind of alliance, a common community.

The *Economic Observer* quickly became very influential. We wrote articles that were pretentiously academic, and so many business figures liked reading them. That came from a shared cultural background, a shared education. Generally speaking, people then longed for and looked up to elite culture. Whereas the past decade has basically been a community around popular culture — whoever you are, you express yourself in language that is excessively down-to-earth.

![Image from [Economic Observer Online](http://www.eeo.com.cn/zt/2009sq/)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20190318233446owWk29ITyzqxuYbA.jpg-w600)

**Q: By "elite" do you mean a concentration of knowledge, or of wealth?**

Knowledge, of course. Ideas. We had no money then.

**Q: What do you make of the phrase "knowledge heroes," which was so popular in the 1990s?**

Right, that was a turn too. *Knowledge Heroes* (《知识英雄》), the book by Liu Ren. That was the first time knowledge and wealth were explicitly connected. Before that no one thought knowledge and wealth had anything to do with each other. In China, knowledge lived in the world of knowledge and business lived in the world of business. That was the moment they joined.

Looking back now, of course, the "knowledge" of that time was only one kind of knowledge, the kind more closely tied to wealth. But things really did change. Successful business today really is mostly about processing information — it just isn't the humanistic knowledge we had in mind. Humanistic knowledge has instead moved further and further to the margins.

People weren't so clear about it then. They thought all knowledge could be converted. So it was a very optimistic time.

**Q: When Wang Zhidong was later pushed off the board, you wrote a piece agreeing with the view that prevailed at the time — that this was the end of adolescence.**

The original founder had to give way to a more mature system and management. Shareholders' interests, the will of capital — the founder had to submit to that will. There was a war between them, a conflict, and the original founder, the more idealistic figure, was pushed out.

**Q: You compared Wang Zhidong to Steve Jobs.**

Ah, I was 24, 25 then. What did I know? I just wrote whatever came into my head. I said I hoped he'd get a second act. Steve Jobs was pushed out too. Analogies are never exact, and even less so when you're young — there's no precision, it's all intuition.

**Q: What was Peking University's centennial like in 1998?**

Quite lively. Officialdom had already begun to take it over, but there was still a relatively free atmosphere. Yu Jie came up around then. There was a group of independent, liberal intellectuals who were quite active — Zhu Xueqin, Liu Junning — and a lot of Hayek's books came out. '97, '98, you could call it a relatively open era with active thinking. People didn't understand business, but they trusted the market economy, and to some degree they believed in the end of history… Given the current climate of opinion I can't put it that way either — anyway, you can't say it fully.

**Q: When you first got to Peking University, your idea of the place seems to have been something else.**

I lived in the Peking University of 1920 and the Peking University of 1980. I lived in those two periods, not in the real Peking University.

**Q: By the time you were there, internet culture had already become a craze. You said everyone was chasing it. What was the atmosphere?**

They all wanted to get into a big company, to do something connected to the internet. Going to Sohu or Sina, or into IBM or HP, were all serious options. The conditions for starting a company didn't exist then. There was no venture capital platform; that came later, when suddenly there was enough money everywhere that getting 500,000 or a few million yuan was normal, a small matter. How could that have happened back then?

Media too. *Computer World* (《计算机世界》) and *China Computer World* (《中国计算机报》) were very popular then. *PC Life* was the same, wasn't it? I went there following Wang Feng, to make a bit of pocket money. Nothing more than that.

**Q: Why do you seem so unwilling to talk about 1999, or about your own past?**

What is there to talk about? I've written it all down. My memory hasn't grown any clearer than it was when I wrote about it, and those experiences haven't become more important, so there's no need to think about them.

**Q: One Way Street raised money in 2013. You also go to events as an entrepreneur. You must have changed too. What changes have you seen in the startup atmosphere?**

I was somewhat skeptical of this wave of startups from the beginning. How to put it… when something becomes too fashionable, I get suspicious. What was in fashion when I started my company? Let me think… The big companies were already very successful, of course; BAT was already solid. What was in fashion? Huang Taiji, right? Yes — "Internet Plus," the internet concept. I was skeptical from the start. I thought, how could things happen this easily?

And I really dislike startup culture. It turns itself into self-heroism, self-romanticization. It exaggerates the bitterness, exaggerates the difficulty, and becomes a strange state of mind. In fact it's an ordinary thing.

**Q: Was the startup culture the same for the 1999 generation?**

That generation was already very successful; otherwise they'd have stopped. I saw more of them around 2000, when I was doing the newspaper. I remember having coffee with Jack Ma and the others at Fuxingmen in 2002. I just thought, this man is a wonderful talker — but I had no idea what Alibaba did. I only knew he was one of the new internet entrepreneurs. Nothing more.

The changes all came abruptly after 2007, 2008, when they turned into companies of enormous scale. Before that I didn't feel it strongly.

The people who started companies in the late 1990s — not all of them, but the main ones — all became empire builders, creators of an empire.

Honestly, Jack Ma, Pony Ma and their generation are a lot like the Rockefellers and Morgans of the digital age. This generation built a huge empire, and the generations after them no longer had that chance. In history only a few generations get such a chance — when railroads were first being laid, when oil and coal were first found, or when the printing press was first made. That kind of possibility existed, and they caught it. That's why their success is jaw-dropping.

![John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil in 1870; at its height it controlled 90% of America's oil market. Rockefeller was the first billionaire in history. Image from [Wikipedia](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%BA%A6%E7%BF%B0%C2%B7%E6%88%B4%E7%BB%B4%E6%A3%AE%C2%B7%E6%B4%9B%E5%85%8B%E8%8F%B2%E5%8B%92#/media/File:John_D._Rockefeller_1885.jpg)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20190318232811xPVMpkR820QHUBwF.jpg-w600)

We're still moving toward a digital society, and new products and new people keep appearing, but they no longer have the chances those empire builders had. That's the big difference.

I'm not especially familiar with them, actually. I don't know them well.

But I think Wang Xing and people like him are impressive too, able to build a smaller empire all over again. Groupon, and Momo… I'm fairly cold to it, honestly. I realized their importance quite late. I was skeptical at first too. So I'm not someone with a fine sense for shifts in business. Fundamentally I'm not sensitive to it, and not that interested either.

I'm still looking for the meaning behind business. In the late 1990s the internet's arrival in China had enormous value as enlightenment. This wave, the mobile internet, produced new social relationships — that came after Facebook — so what do these new human relationships actually mean? Yes, I've always been more interested in the social impact behind business and technology.

**Q: What social impact did 1999 have?**

An enormous one, obviously. I think that from the late 1990s on, for a decade or more, Chinese society was in a moment of very active commerce, of commerce swelling and growing fast, and that had a great deal to do with internet technology. Society's learning curve, the way it reorganized itself, was closely tied to this technological revolution.

I think that after the late 1990s, America's influence on the world became commercial and technological, and entertainment — the direct impact of things like Hollywood movies — no longer an impact on thought and culture. So America's technological, commercial and entertainment vocabularies became extremely powerful, dominant.

Over the past three or four years, because of the growth of China's mobile internet, a lot of people feel China no longer loses to America, that America has lost its aura. Behind that is partly the result of media and opinion steering; they've been encouraging a certain sentiment, and the tilt gradually shifts, until people can no longer talk about America fairly. And over the past four or five years, public opinion has developed a blind self-satisfaction.

Some of that is normal. Once a country rises, its view of the outside world gradually changes. In Emerson's America there was blind worship of Britain, blind worship of Europe, so Emerson reminded them: Americans, you must observe with your own eyes, walk on your own feet, think with your own mind. It's the same for China; we need that too. But this more independent thinking, this fairer observation, has to be built on honesty, not on technology for distorting information.

**Q: How is this different from the mood behind the 1990s bestseller *China Can Say No* (《中国可以说不》)?**

…That one was more defensive; this one is more offensive. The whole subject is tiresome — if you go around certain things, any discussion of it is empty talk. What matters most underneath is what role the "elephant in the room" is playing.

**Q: Changing subject: how did the 1999 wave of company-building differ from the 1992 wave?**

1999 was a huge upgrade. It brought technology and money in step with the outside world: you took money from American venture capital and used their newest technical tools and ways of working directly. 1992 was still about activating domestic commercial circulation. Lots of small factories, a small industrial revolution, but at the downstream end of the whole manufacturing chain. It was part of China entering a more global market.

1999 was smaller in scale, but it started out relatively in step with the world. It was the first time China was more or less synchronized with a global technological revolution. In the past few years people have come to think we're a global leader, at least in mobile payments and mobile more broadly, and that huge shift in mentality is also a big reason attitudes toward the West have changed.

But what I mean is, China has such enormous resources and potential that with fairer policy and better methods it could erupt far more powerfully. I've never seen anyone anywhere in the world who loves producing, and loves consuming, the way Chinese people do.

**Q: How do you read the internet's development over the past 20 years?**

You can pick out a few turning points.

How did China's internet rise? A group of students in America saw that China was getting more and more open after the 1990s, and they brought money back to China and started companies. That's the first stage. The 2000 listings brought American capital in very explicitly, and people saw the myth of wealth — William Ding becoming the richest man in the country so young.

After the bubble burst, those few depressed years were actually when the next wave took shape. Alibaba and Tencent — by around 2007, 2008, they had built the new BAT.

At first the internet was just a new space; people shared information and that was enough. Then when mouse and bricks really joined together — Alibaba selling goods is the classic case — the internet world was grafted onto the physical world, and a huge new economy was born at once. Behind that, it lined up perfectly with China becoming the world's factory. Middle-class consumption began to rise, and Tencent's culture of entertainment consumption joined with it.

After that came the Wall Street crisis, the whole Western economic crisis. The "China model" was born; after the Olympics, they produced a new kind of combination.

After 2008, a stronger state will appeared. After 2012, 2013, another change came, because ideological control was tightening. Everything new was becoming old. The giant BAT companies turned into something like state enterprises with market characteristics, and became very stable. They no longer stood for the newborn thing they'd once been. The whole society started to harden.

After 2013, 2014, it was also a stage of accumulated capital and wealth with nowhere to go. In much of this country that pressure has no outlet. Venture capital is still a small pool of money — a few tens of billions of yuan already makes a splash. There really isn't much money in it, yet it suddenly stirs up a new wave and forms a giant media myth. In reality it isn't nearly that big.

Roughly those waves. Within the process you have to follow a few threads. There's internet companies' own appetite for monopoly and expansion, and there's the government's process of understanding new technology, its own learning curve, how to make it part of its system. In the end it did become part of that system. And there's another thread: the original enlightenment was that individuals win freedom through technology — have individuals won freedom now? Or has technology wrapped people in a new confinement behind a glowing screen?

The core of it, for me, is the relationship between the state and society.

Back in 2003, 2004, the West was already warning that the internet wasn't all freedom and openness, that it had another side, one that could join with power. That has now more or less come true.

And the internet is also a symbol of globalization after the Cold War. Its real expansion came in the 1990s, in an era of the end of history, the end of the US-Soviet Cold War, an era that believed in a world without borders, and it spread across the world quickly against that backdrop. Now people are rebuilding borders: Britain is leaving the EU, nationalism is rising again, trade barriers are appearing between countries again. The West's attitude toward China has changed; it used to very much hope China would become a "stakeholder." In an era like this, the internet is changing too. Look at Russia trying to cut itself off from the global internet.

So for me, the global culture our generation wanted to share is now running into many new barriers. That's the feeling of it.

Google's exit from China matters as well. If Google hadn't left, Baidu wouldn't be this bad. In the online world at least, Chinese people are now subjected to such enormous spiritual pollution — all the worst vocabulary, the worst things mixed together, like an information dump. That's the most striking thing of the past five or six years.

**Q: But some people think that if Google hadn't left China and Facebook hadn't been blocked, Baidu and Tencent wouldn't have grown so well.**

True, but that kind of "well" is at the company level. It isn't what's best at the level of society.

Another thing is that the internet brought a great deal of cultural democracy — democracy in a certain sense, a leveling. In China, political order and economic order are both relatively more fixed, more powerful. So our urge toward equality vented itself in culture instead. That's why, in our internet, elite culture was the first thing destroyed. We entered a state of free-for-all, of anarchy. Nothing higher, nothing lower, everything the same. That's another kind of transfer of social energy.

You have no community of your own, no space to express yourself. Then suddenly, in the online world, everyone can vote, everyone can speak. Because our sense of identity has no outlet in daily life, our internet is especially quick to take sides. Everywhere in the world is quick to take sides, of course, but it's more obvious in China.

**Q: Is starting a company a strong desire for economic equality?**

It may be a continuation of the economic form China has always relied on. In the older commercial era, everyone wanted to open a little shop. Because we lack a form of organization with longer continuity. Japanese companies can last a hundred years, but we lack that form, so small independent things keep springing up.

Startup culture is really the same. From the Wenzhou merchants down to today, everyone is full of that desire. Behind it is the fact that the larger structure isn't stable enough. The second thing is Chinese people's hunger for opportunity, the fear of missing out. Getting off a plane, everyone rushes to be first, grabbing their luggage before the door has even opened.

Cultural life lacks a sense of security and needs more wealth; identity has no chance to prove itself in daily life, and economic activity is the best way to prove yourself. Because in this era, learning can't prove who you are. Neither can a hobby. The only channel of proof is economic success. A black-tier bank credit card can prove you. So everyone is pushed onto a very narrow track of self-proof.

**Q: Do you think the generation born in the 1970s has a particular significance for the first wave of internet entrepreneurship?**

They were the pioneers. The most successful ones, like William Ding, were all born in the '70s; Zhang Chaoyang is a bit older. Robin Li and the others are roughly that age too. They caught the best moment. It's timing — the moment you graduated happened to be this moment.

**Q: That has nothing to do with the education and environment they grew up in?**

Not much connection.

**Q: Zha Jianying interviewed Chen Danqing once, and Chen Danqing was deeply uncomfortable about his own experiences. He said he badly wanted to see what the 1970s generation could ultimately accomplish.**

I love that line of Xu Bing's: "Ignorance as nourishment."
